title: Shift Up Faces Backlash Over AI-Generated K-Pop Music Video for Stellar Blade: Blood Rain
excerpt: The South Korean studio's AI-produced promotional video featuring protagonist Evie has sparked widespread criticism from fans, deepening an ongoing controversy over generative AI use in the hit franchise's sequel.
body:
• Shift Up released an AI-generated K-pop music video titled 'Wanna Be in Love' featuring Stellar Blade: Blood Rain protagonist Evie, drawing immediate criticism from fans and gaming media.
  • The backlash follows earlier AI controversies around the game's Summer Game Fest 2026 reveal trailer, which contained nonsensical AI-generated Chinese characters and distorted architecture.
  • CEO Hyung-tae Kim has publicly endorsed generative AI, claiming 'one person can perform the work of 100 people,' fuelling scrutiny of the studio's creative output.
  • The AI-generated video stands in stark contrast to the original Stellar Blade's 2024 collaboration with real K-pop artist BIBI, which was widely praised.

South Korean game developer Shift Up is facing a wave of online criticism after releasing an AI-generated K-pop music video to promote Stellar Blade: Blood Rain, the sequel to its 2024 action hit. The promotional video, titled "Wanna Be in Love," features the game's new protagonist Evie performing a pop number set against the upcoming title's China-inspired cityscape — and fans are not impressed.

"I feel profoundly disappointed," one commenter wrote, according to Push Square, which reported that the studio was being "utterly roasted on social media" over the release. Kotaku noted that "even Stellar Blade fans" — a community known for its fierce loyalty to the franchise — "couldn't stomach" the video, while TheGamer called the release "embarrassing."

A Deepening AI Controversy

The music video is the latest flashpoint in what has become a recurring debate around Shift Up's embrace of generative AI technology. When the studio unveiled Stellar Blade: Blood Rain at Summer Game Fest in June 2026, fans and analysts quickly identified telltale signs of AI-generated content in both the reveal trailer and key art.

Chinese-speaking players spotted nonsensical characters on in-game signage — text that did not correspond to any real language — a common artefact of AI image generation. Daniel Camilo of GamesIndustry.biz described the AI elements as "sloppy" and noted they were "not a good look" for a reveal trailer, even as placeholders.

"We devote around 150 people to a single game, but China puts in between 1,000 to 2,000. We lack the capacity to compete, both in terms of quality and volume of content."

— Hyung-tae Kim, CEO, Shift Up

Shift Up CEO and Stellar Blade director Hyung-tae Kim has been openly enthusiastic about AI's role in game development. Speaking at South Korea's "2026 Economic Growth Strategy" conference in January — attended by President Lee Jae Myung — Kim argued that generative AI and large language models could help smaller Korean studios compete with China's massive development teams. His assertion that AI enables "one person to perform the work of 100 people" has since become a lightning rod for criticism.

From BIBI to AI: A Jarring Contrast

The backlash is amplified by the contrast with the original Stellar Blade's promotional strategy. In April 2024, Shift Up and Sony Interactive Entertainment partnered with BIBI, a rising K-pop star, for a critically praised music video titled "Eve" that coincided with the game's PS5 launch. That collaboration featured a real artist performing an original song, with production values that matched the game's polished aesthetic.

The decision to replace a genuine K-pop collaboration with an AI-generated video for the sequel has struck many fans as a step backward. "Where's the artistry?" was a recurring refrain on social media, according to Push Square's coverage.

High Stakes for a Hit Franchise

The controversy carries real commercial stakes. The original Stellar Blade has sold over three million copies across PS5 and PC, with analytics firm Gamalytic revealing that more than 60 percent of its PC audience came from China — the very market where AI-generated Chinese signage in promotional materials could prove most damaging.

Shift Up plans to self-publish Blood Rain rather than going through Sony Interactive Entertainment, as it did with the original. While the company has praised Sony's publishing support, Kim has said self-publishing allows the studio to be "more nimble and agile." The game, which introduces a new protagonist named Evie in a Chongqing-inspired setting, was revealed at Summer Game Fest but has no confirmed release date and is believed to be several years from launch.

A Broader Industry Tension

Shift Up's situation reflects a wider tension across the gaming industry. Studios are increasingly experimenting with generative AI to reduce costs and speed up production, but player communities have grown increasingly hostile toward perceived "AI slop" in commercial releases. Just this week, Square Enix was forced to clarify that Kingdom Hearts artwork accused of using generative AI was the result of "regular human error," illustrating how sensitive the issue has become.

For Indian gaming fans and the broader diaspora tech community, the controversy highlights a debate that extends well beyond gaming. South Korea's push to integrate AI across its creative industries mirrors similar discussions in India's tech sector, where the balance between AI efficiency and creative integrity is an increasingly urgent question. The K-pop connection adds another layer: K-pop's global fan base, which includes a significant Indian following, has traditionally valued authentic artistry and high production values — standards an AI-generated music video struggles to meet.

Shift Up has not publicly responded to the latest criticism. Whether the studio adjusts its marketing approach ahead of Blood Rain's eventual release remains to be seen, but the message from its fanbase is clear: for a franchise built on visual craftsmanship, AI-generated promotional content is a hard sell.
